label: PART IV
title: Reusable Design Shapes
lead: Use patterns as shared vocabulary for recurring forces, not as trophies to insert into every design.

chapters.title: Creational patterns
chapters.intro: Creational patterns separate what an object does from how a suitable instance is selected or assembled.

concepts.title: Factory Method
concepts.definition: Let a creator's overridable method choose the concrete product while the creator keeps the surrounding workflow stable.
concepts.look_for: A base workflow is reusable, but one object it creates must vary with the creator subtype or extension point.
concepts.walkthrough: `ReportExporter.Export`/`export` owns the stable workflow: obtain an encoder, encode the report, then write the bytes. `CreateEncoder`/`create_encoder` is the Factory Method. `JsonReportExporter` returns a `JsonReportEncoder`, while `CsvReportExporter` returns a `CsvReportEncoder`; the workflow consumes both through `IReportEncoder` or the equivalent Python protocol. Product creation varies by creator subtype without placing format switches inside `Export`. This GoF pattern is more specific than any method that happens to construct an object. A static `UserAccount.Register` is also commonly called a factory method in everyday conversation, but it does not use subclass override to extend a surrounding algorithm. When inheritance exists only to select one constructor, injecting an encoder factory or encoder instance is usually simpler. Factory Method earns its hierarchy when creator specialization and workflow reuse belong together.
concepts.caution: Do not introduce a creator hierarchy solely to avoid one constructor call. Prefer direct construction or an injected factory when no reusable creator workflow exists.
concepts.related: Template Method often contains the factory method. Abstract Factory creates a compatible family rather than one product selected inside a creator workflow.

concepts.title: Abstract Factory
concepts.definition: Provide one contract for creating a compatible family of related products without naming concrete product classes at use sites.
concepts.look_for: Several objects must be selected as a matching set, such as platform controls, provider-specific database components, or environment clients.
concepts.walkthrough: `IUiFactory`/`UiFactory` creates two related product roles: a button and a dialog. `WindowsUiFactory` returns the Windows implementations as a family; `MacUiFactory` returns the matching Mac family. `SettingsScreen` receives one factory and never names `WindowsButton`, `MacDialog`, or any other concrete product, so configuration selects the platform once and incompatible mixtures are harder to create. The axis of variation is the product family, not each object independently. Adding a Linux family means implementing the existing creation methods. Adding a brand-new product role, such as `CreateMenu`, is expensive because every factory must change; that is the characteristic Abstract Factory trade-off. If products do not need to match, independent factories or direct dependency injection are simpler and allow choices to vary separately.
concepts.caution: Use a family factory only when compatibility across products is a real invariant. Every new product role changes all concrete factories.
concepts.related: Factory Method creates one product through an extension point. Builder assembles one complex result across steps.

concepts.title: Builder
concepts.definition: Assemble a complex object step by step, keeping readable construction and completion-time validation separate from the final representation.
concepts.look_for: Construction has many optional parts, meaningful sequencing, reusable recipes, or invariants that can be checked only when assembly finishes.
concepts.walkthrough: `ReportDefinitionBuilder` owns mutable assembly state while `ReportDefinition` can remain a completed, stable value. `WithTitle`, `AddColumn`, and `GroupBy` name construction steps; `Build` verifies that the title and at least one column exist, then copies the columns into the result. The C# client uses fluent chaining, while the expanded Python client shows the same calls separately so sequencing remains obvious. The builder is useful because validation depends on the assembled combination and repeated columns make a constructor awkward. Named arguments, object initializers, records, and dataclasses are simpler when construction is just optional data assignment. A builder earns its extra type when it supports meaningful recipes, staged validation, ordered steps, or multiple representations. Reusing a mutable builder also needs a documented reset policy; creating a fresh builder per product is safest.
concepts.caution: Do not replace a clear constructor with ceremonial fluent calls. Define whether builders are reusable, and copy mutable collections into the built object.
concepts.related: Abstract Factory selects a family; Builder controls assembly of one result. Fluent Interface describes the chaining syntax, not the construction responsibility.

concepts.title: Prototype
concepts.definition: Create a new object by copying a representative instance whose configuration is already useful, then change only what differs.
concepts.look_for: Initial configuration is expensive or verbose, and the domain can define clearly which nested values are copied versus shared.
concepts.walkthrough: `standardLayout` is the prototype. `Clone`/`clone` creates another `DashboardLayout` with the same configuration, explicitly cloning each `Widget`; the client then changes only the new layout's name. That avoids repeating a verbose dashboard recipe and lets runtime-created configurations serve as templates. Copy semantics are the central design decision. The example deep-copies widgets so edits in `teamLayout` do not mutate `standardLayout`. Immutable widget definitions could instead be shared safely, while resources such as database connections should rarely be copied at all. Generic `MemberwiseClone`, `copy.copy`, or serialization cloning can hide these decisions and produce accidental aliasing. Prototype is valuable when the representative instance carries meaningful configuration; a straightforward constructor or factory is clearer when creation is cheap and the required arguments are already known.
concepts.caution: Document copy depth and ownership for every nested object. Shallow copies can share mutable children, locks, handles, or subscriptions unexpectedly.
concepts.related: A registry often stores named prototypes. Factory methods can choose which prototype to clone without exposing concrete types.

concepts.title: Singleton
concepts.definition: Maintain one instance of a service within a deliberate scope; modern code usually lets a composition root or container own that lifetime instead of exposing a global accessor.
concepts.look_for: A stateless or process-scoped infrastructure service must be shared consistently, and its single-instance lifetime is an explicit operational choice.
concepts.walkthrough: The composition root constructs one `SystemClock` and passes that same instance to `TokenService` and `AuditService`. The C# container shorthand expresses the same application-scoped lifetime through `AddSingleton`; the container creates one `IClock` implementation and reuses it for dependents. This modern form preserves explicit constructor dependencies and lets tests supply another clock. The classic GoF implementation combines controlled construction, a static stored instance, and global `Instance` access. That shape makes dependencies invisible, complicates tests, and often turns mutable state into process-wide coupling. A container-managed singleton is still one object per container, not necessarily one object per machine, tenant, or cluster. The scope must match the resource: request-scoped state is not a singleton, and distributed uniqueness requires coordination beyond an in-process pattern.
concepts.caution: Global reachability is the main hazard. Keep dependencies explicit, avoid mutable shared state, and define whether 'one' means per container, process, tenant, or deployment.
concepts.related: Dependency Injection manages lifetime without global access. Monostate shares state across instances but has many of the same global-state problems.
concepts.modern_note: Treat singleton primarily as a lifetime decision. A DI container's singleton registration is usually safer than a static `Instance` property.

chapters.title: Structural patterns
chapters.intro: Structural patterns arrange objects and interfaces so incompatible or changing parts can collaborate through stable shapes.

concepts.title: Adapter
concepts.definition: Translate an existing interface into the contract a client expects while preserving the underlying capability's meaning.
concepts.look_for: A legacy, vendor, protocol, or platform component provides the needed behavior through incompatible names, types, or units.
concepts.walkthrough: `FreezeMonitor` expects a sensor that reports Celsius through `ReadCelsius`/`read_celsius`. `LegacyFahrenheitSensor` offers the same physical observation through an incompatible method and unit. `FahrenheitSensorAdapter` holds the legacy sensor, invokes `CurrentTemperatureFahrenheit`, performs the conversion, and presents the expected contract. The client remains unaware of the vendor type and can also accept a native Celsius sensor. The adapter owns translation at the boundary; it should not invent domain policy unrelated to compatibility. Unit conversion is mathematically lossy only to the chosen numeric precision, which should be documented if thresholds are sensitive. Adapter differs from Decorator: a decorator preserves the same interface while adding behavior, whereas this adapter changes the interface seen by the client.
concepts.caution: Verify semantic compatibility, units, error behavior, and precision. An adapter cannot make fundamentally different meanings interchangeable.
concepts.related: Facade simplifies a subsystem rather than targeting one expected contract. Anti-Corruption Layer is a broader domain-level translation boundary.

concepts.title: Bridge
concepts.definition: Separate two independently varying dimensions into composed abstractions so their combinations do not require a subclass for each pair.
concepts.look_for: Two axes such as report type and output format are multiplying classes into combinations like HTML sales, CSV sales, HTML inventory, and CSV inventory.
concepts.walkthrough: The report abstraction and the formatting implementation are separate dimensions joined by composition. `SalesReport` and `InventoryReport` decide which titles and rows constitute two different reports. `HtmlReportFormatter` and `PlainTextReportFormatter` decide how either report becomes a document. The client combines HTML with sales and plain text with inventory without creating `HtmlSalesReport`, `PlainTextSalesReport`, `HtmlInventoryReport`, and `PlainTextInventoryReport` subclasses. Any of the four combinations is available at construction time, so each axis evolves independently. In Bridge terminology, `Report` is the abstraction, `IReportFormatter` is the implementor, and their concrete descendants supply the two variations. Ordinary composition is enough when only one side varies; the Bridge name becomes useful when both sides form meaningful, independently evolving families. The price is more indirection and a formatter contract that must support every report without leaking format-specific assumptions.
concepts.caution: Do not invoke Bridge for every composed object. Use it when two real axes vary independently and combination subclasses would otherwise proliferate.
concepts.related: Strategy also composes behavior, usually along one policy axis. Adapter reconciles incompatible existing contracts rather than separating two planned dimensions.

concepts.title: Composite
concepts.definition: Give leaves and containers the same operation so clients can treat individual objects and nested groups uniformly as a tree.
concepts.look_for: The domain contains part-whole trees such as files and folders, UI elements, expressions, organizations, or nested work items.
concepts.python_shorthand:
def size_in_bytes(self):
    return sum(child.size_in_bytes() for child in self._children)
concepts.walkthrough: `FileNode` is a leaf: `SizeInBytes`/`size_in_bytes` returns its own byte count. `Folder` is a composite: it holds other `IFileSystemNode` objects, asks each child for its size, and totals the results. Because a child may be another folder, the same operation recurses through an arbitrarily deep tree. The client builds `project` from one file and a nested `images` folder, then asks the root for its size without distinguishing leaf from container. The LINQ and generator-expression shorthands compress the explicit accumulation after the recursion is understood. A useful component interface contains only operations meaningful for both leaves and composites. Putting `Add` on `IFileSystemNode` would force files to reject an operation they cannot support; keeping it on `Folder` avoids that transparent-but-unsafe variant of Composite. Cycles must also be prevented or traversal guarded, because the pattern assumes a tree.
concepts.caution: Keep the shared contract genuinely uniform, control child mutation, and prevent cycles when recursion assumes a tree.
concepts.related: Iterator can traverse a composite without exposing representation. Visitor can add operations across node types when the node structure is stable.

concepts.title: Decorator
concepts.definition: Decorator adds behavior around an object by wrapping it in another object that implements the same contract. Callers can keep using the contract while wrappers are composed independently of the underlying implementation.
concepts.look_for: Use it when several optional concerns - such as logging, caching, authorization, or retries - must surround the same operation in different combinations.
concepts.walkthrough: `LoggingPriceSource` and `CatalogPriceSource` both satisfy `IPriceSource`, so the caller does not need a special API for the wrapped version. `LoggingPriceSource.GetPrice` performs work before and after delegating to `_inner.GetPrice`; it adds logging without editing `CatalogPriceSource`. Another wrapper, such as `CachingPriceSource`, could receive either the catalog source or the logging wrapper. That ability to stack same-contract wrappers is the defining Decorator move. The axis of variation is the set and order of surrounding behaviors, while the price lookup contract remains stable. This differs from a proxy mainly by intent: both may have the same shape, but a proxy controls access to a particular subject, whereas decorators are deliberately composed to add responsibilities. It also differs from ordinary inheritance because each wrapper is selected and combined at runtime. Python relies on structural compatibility rather than a declared interface, but the delegation is the same.
concepts.caution: Wrapper order is observable: caching outside logging records only cache misses, while logging outside caching records every request. Keep stacks short, document their order, and avoid wrappers that silently change the core contract.

concepts.title: Façade (Facade)
concepts.definition: A facade presents a small, task-oriented API over a more complicated subsystem. It hides routine coordination without requiring every lower-level capability to disappear.
concepts.look_for: Use it when many callers repeat the same multi-step workflow or must understand several subsystem APIs just to perform one common task.
concepts.python_expanded:
class CheckoutFacade:
    def __init__(self, inventory, payments, receipts):
        self._inventory = inventory
        self._payments = payments
        self._receipts = receipts

    async def place_order(self, order):
        await self._inventory.reserve(order.lines)
        await self._payments.charge(order.customer_id, order.total)
        await self._receipts.send(order)


checkout = CheckoutFacade(inventory, payments, receipts)
await checkout.place_order(order)
concepts.walkthrough: The caller asks `CheckoutFacade.PlaceOrderAsync` to complete one business-facing task instead of coordinating `InventoryService`, `PaymentService`, and `ReceiptService` itself. The facade knows the normal sequence - reserve, charge, then send a receipt - while the collaborators retain their focused responsibilities. This gives common callers a stable entry point even if subsystem APIs or orchestration details change. A facade does not necessarily replace those lower-level APIs; an administrative tool may still call `InventoryService` directly when it truly needs that control. The pattern is about simplifying access, not disguising one object behind the same interface. That distinction separates Facade from Proxy and Decorator. It can resemble a Mediator because both coordinate objects, but a facade is chiefly an outward-facing convenience boundary; a mediator chiefly governs communication among peers. The Python version makes the same responsibility split without static contracts.
concepts.caution: A facade becomes a god object when business rules and every exceptional workflow accumulate inside it. Keep it focused on a cohesive set of use cases and leave domain decisions with their proper owners.

concepts.title: Flyweight
concepts.definition: Flyweight reduces memory use by sharing immutable intrinsic state among many logical objects while keeping per-instance, extrinsic state elsewhere.
concepts.look_for: Consider it only after profiling shows that a very large population repeats the same substantial values, such as glyph shapes, styles, or map-tile definitions.
concepts.walkthrough: `FontStyle` contains intrinsic state: the family, size, and weight can be shared safely because the object is immutable. Coordinates and text remain extrinsic state on each `Word`, because those values differ from word to word. `FontStyleFactory.Get` returns the same `FontStyle` instance for the same key, so thousands of words need not each allocate an identical style. The factory or cache is helpful infrastructure, but sharing the repeated intrinsic value is what makes this Flyweight. The shorthand versions use standard cache helpers; the C# lambda is a value factory whose target type is inferred by `GetOrAdd`, and `static` guarantees it captures no surrounding state. Python's `setdefault` is compact but eagerly constructs its default, so it is not equivalent for expensive values; the expanded factory is clearer and safer in that case. Flyweight pays off only when saved memory outweighs lookup and indirection costs.
concepts.caution: Never share mutable flyweight state unless mutation is rigorously synchronized and intended for every user. Measure retained memory first; a cache can consume more memory than it saves and needs an eviction policy if keys are unbounded.
concepts.modern_note: Records and immutable value types make intrinsic state easier to express, but immutability alone does not create sharing.

concepts.title: Proxy
concepts.definition: A proxy stands in for another object through the same contract and controls access to that subject for authorization, lazy loading, remoting, caching, or lifecycle management.
concepts.look_for: Use it when callers should see the subject's normal API but every access must cross a policy, location, or lifecycle boundary.
concepts.walkthrough: `AuthorizedDocumentStore` implements the same `IDocumentStore` contract as `databaseStore`, so clients call `Load` without learning a second access API. Before forwarding to `_inner.Load`, the proxy asks `_user.CanRead` whether the current request may cross the boundary. The subject remains responsible for loading documents; the proxy owns access control. That controlled substitution is the essence of Proxy. Its class shape resembles Decorator, but the intent is different: this wrapper represents and governs access to a subject rather than serving as one freely stackable enhancement among many. A remote proxy may also serialize a call or a virtual proxy may defer creating an expensive object. Those versions should expose asynchronous and failure behavior honestly rather than making network or disk access appear indistinguishable from a cheap local property. Python obtains substitutability by convention unless a `Protocol` or abstract base class is added.
concepts.caution: A proxy can hide cost, latency, and failure. Avoid sync-looking APIs for remote work, and make authorization decisions with trusted server-side context rather than caller-supplied claims.

chapters.title: Behavioral patterns
chapters.intro: Behavioral patterns distribute decisions and communication among objects without hard-wiring every participant to every other one.

concepts.title: Chain of Responsibility
concepts.definition: Chain of Responsibility sends a request through an ordered series of handlers. A handler may satisfy the request, reject it, or pass it onward, depending on the chain's contract.
concepts.look_for: Use it when validators, middleware, parsers, authorization checks, or fallbacks should be independently composed and reordered.
concepts.walkthrough: `Handle` visits `IRequestHandler` instances in their configured order. `CachedRequestHandler.TryHandle` returns a `HandlingResult` on a cache hit and `null` when the next handler should get a chance. A database handler could follow it, then a remote fallback. `Handle` owns traversal and the no-handler policy; each handler owns one way to respond. The collection can change without editing the individual handlers, which makes composition the axis of variation. Some chains instead require every handler to contribute and call the next one, as HTTP middleware often does; that is still the pattern, but the continuation contract must be explicit. The shorthand versions replace handler objects with callables. In C#, the named `Handler` delegate states the target signature; lambdas could populate the list, but they are not necessary to understand the pattern. Chain of Responsibility differs from Decorator because a request may stop at one handler rather than necessarily flowing through every wrapper.
concepts.caution: Ordering and termination are part of the behavior even when configuration hides them. Test the assembled chain, define what `null` or continuation means, and decide explicitly what happens when nobody handles the request.

concepts.title: Command
concepts.definition: Command packages a request and its required data as a first-class object so execution can have a lifecycle separate from the caller that created it.
concepts.look_for: Use it when an operation must be queued, scheduled, logged, retried, authorized, recorded for undo, or dispatched independently of its invoker.
concepts.python_expanded:
class SendReceiptCommand:
    def __init__(self, order, email_sender):
        self._order = order
        self._email_sender = email_sender

    async def execute(self):
        await self._email_sender.send(
            self._order.email_address,
            "Your receipt",
        )


command = SendReceiptCommand(order, email_sender)
await command_queue.enqueue(command)
concepts.walkthrough: `SendReceiptCommand` captures the `Order` and `IEmailSender` needed to perform one request. The producer creates the command and hands it to `commandQueue`; it does not have to execute the email operation immediately. The queue can schedule, persist, retry, or audit commands through the common `ICommand.ExecuteAsync` contract. `SendReceiptCommand` still owns the semantics of sending this particular receipt, while the invoker owns when and under what policy execution occurs. That separated lifecycle is what distinguishes Command from simply extracting a method. A plain callable can serve as a lightweight command inside one process, but a named object is usually clearer when the request needs identity, serialization, validation, undo data, or durable transport. In distributed systems, do not serialize service objects such as `_emailSender`; persist command data and resolve infrastructure dependencies in the consumer instead.
concepts.caution: Command objects add ceremony when execution is immediate and needs no independent policy. Durable commands also need versioning, idempotency, and a clear answer for partial failure.
concepts.modern_note: Frameworks often call every request message a command. In domain usage, reserve command for an intent to change state; a query asks for information.

concepts.title: Iterator
concepts.definition: Iterator provides sequential access to elements without exposing the collection's representation or forcing callers to manage traversal state.
concepts.look_for: Use the language's iteration protocol first; implement a custom iterator when traversal is lazy, filtered, paged, stateful, or structurally nontrivial.
concepts.walkthrough: `DepthFirst` owns the `pending` stack and therefore the bookkeeping for tree traversal. Its caller sees an ordinary sequence of `Node` values and can use `foreach` or `for` without knowing whether the tree is represented recursively, iteratively, or even fetched page by page. Each `yield return` or `yield` suspends the iterator while preserving its state, so nodes are produced lazily rather than accumulated into a second collection. The shorthand versions express the same depth-first order recursively; `yield from` in Python delegates iteration to the child generator, while C# spells out the nested enumeration. Iterator is the protocol and traversal object; a generator is a language mechanism that lets the compiler construct that iterator for you. Because enumeration controls when work happens, the contract should say whether a sequence can be replayed and whether moving to the next element can perform I/O or fail.
concepts.caution: Lazy iterators can keep files, database readers, or mutable collections alive longer than expected. Document one-shot behavior, dispose resources correctly, and avoid hiding remote I/O behind an apparently cheap synchronous enumeration.
concepts.modern_note: Use `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` or an async generator when obtaining each element is genuinely asynchronous.

concepts.title: Mediator
concepts.definition: Mediator gives a bounded collaboration one coordinator, allowing participating objects to communicate through it instead of depending directly on every peer.
concepts.look_for: Use it when peer-to-peer links form a web and one component can clearly own the workflow or interaction protocol.
concepts.python_expanded:
class CheckoutMediator:
    def __init__(self, inventory, payments):
        self._inventory = inventory
        self._payments = payments

    async def place(self, order):
        await self._inventory.reserve(order.id, order.lines)
        await self._payments.charge(order.id, order.total)
        order.mark_placed()


await mediator.place(order)
concepts.walkthrough: `CheckoutMediator.PlaceAsync` defines how `InventoryService`, `PaymentService`, and `Order` collaborate to place an order. Inventory does not call payments, payments does not mutate the order, and the order does not know either service. Each participant depends on the mediator's protocol rather than accumulating links to every peer. The mediator therefore owns sequencing, while reservation, charging, and the order transition remain with their respective owners. This is useful when changing the collaboration - perhaps inserting fraud approval between reservation and charging - should not force several components to learn about one another. Mediator can look almost identical to a Facade in a tiny example. The distinction is viewpoint: a facade simplifies an interface for outside clients; a mediator is the authority for communication among participants. One object may play both roles, but naming the intent prevents the coordinator from becoming an arbitrary home for business logic.
concepts.caution: A mediator can turn into a god object or a message bus that hides all control flow. Keep its scope cohesive, preserve logic in domain owners, and resist routing every call through one global mediator.

concepts.title: Memento
concepts.definition: Memento captures enough of an object's state to restore it later while keeping the object's internal representation under that object's control.
concepts.look_for: Use it for undo, drafts, checkpoints, or transactional editing when a state snapshot is affordable and restoration has clear semantics.
concepts.walkthrough: `Document.Save` decides which internal state belongs in a `DocumentSnapshot`; the caretaker merely stores the returned snapshot. Later, `Document.Restore` interprets that snapshot and returns `Text` to its earlier value. The caller never reaches into private fields or reconstructs the document itself, so encapsulation survives the undo feature. `DocumentSnapshot` is immutable, preventing an old checkpoint from changing underneath the history. The snapshot is the memento, `Document` is the originator, and the code holding `beforeEdit` is the caretaker in classic terminology. The C# record is a concise modern representation of the same immutable value; it does not change the roles. Memento differs from Command-based undo: a memento records state, while an undoable command records an operation and often its inverse. Snapshots are simple when state is small; operation logs or structural sharing may scale better for large documents.
concepts.caution: Snapshots can retain large graphs, sensitive values, or references that become invalid after external changes. Define snapshot scope and versioning, and do not assume restoring in-memory state can reverse an external side effect.

concepts.title: Observer
concepts.definition: Observer lets a subject publish a notification to registered subscribers without depending on their concrete types.
concepts.look_for: Use it for optional in-process reactions when one state change has several listeners that may be added or removed independently.
concepts.walkthrough: `Order` knows only that `Placed` has subscribers; it does not know about `receiptListener` or any other concrete reaction. `Place` first commits the order's own state change, then `OnPlaced` invokes a snapshot of the event delegate. The subscription line connects `receiptListener.HandleOrderPlaced` without modifying `Order`, so adding analytics or UI refresh listeners changes the observer set rather than the subject. In classic terms, `Order` is the subject and the subscribed handlers are observers. The C# shorthand uses a statement lambda as an anonymous event handler: the event's `EventHandler<OrderPlacedEventArgs>` type supplies the parameter types, and the lambda captures `receiptService`. A named method is easier to unsubscribe and usually better for nontrivial behavior. Observer is synchronous and in-process here; a durable message broker adds delivery, ordering, and failure semantics that this example does not provide.
concepts.caution: Notifications create indirect control flow. Specify ordering and exception behavior, unsubscribe long-lived publishers from short-lived listeners, and do not confuse an in-memory event with reliable cross-process messaging.
concepts.modern_note: In .NET, weak events or explicit `IDisposable` subscriptions can reduce lifetime leaks in long-lived UI publishers.

concepts.title: State
concepts.definition: State moves lifecycle-dependent behavior into state objects so an object changes behavior by changing its current state rather than growing conditionals across many methods.
concepts.look_for: Use it when several operations vary by lifecycle state and transitions form a meaningful state machine that keeps expanding.
concepts.walkthrough: `Order` delegates `Pay` and `Ship` to its current `_state`, then stores the state returned by that operation. `AwaitingPaymentState.Pay` permits the transition to `PaidState`, while `AwaitingPaymentState.Ship` rejects an invalid transition. `PaidState` answers the same operations differently. The public `Order` API stays stable as states and transition rules grow; behavior varies with lifecycle state rather than with a policy chosen by the caller. That last point distinguishes State from Strategy. Both delegate through a common contract, but a Strategy is normally supplied as an interchangeable algorithm, whereas State changes as the context moves through its lifecycle and state objects often determine valid transitions. For a small workflow, an enum and an explicit transition table may communicate the entire machine more clearly. State earns its extra types when behavior is substantial across multiple operations, not merely because one `switch` exists.
concepts.caution: Scattering transition creation among state classes can make the complete state machine difficult to audit. Keep transitions explicit, test illegal paths, and consider centralizing transition policy when global visibility matters.
concepts.related: Strategy; Finite-State Machine; Replace Type Code with State/Strategy

concepts.title: Strategy
concepts.definition: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind one contract and lets a client or context select the policy to use.
concepts.look_for: Use it when the main workflow is stable but one calculation, ordering rule, routing policy, or other algorithm must vary independently.
concepts.python_shorthand:
total = calculate_total(
    prices,
    lambda subtotal: subtotal * Decimal("0.90"),
)
concepts.walkthrough: `TotalCalculator.Calculate` owns the stable workflow: add `prices`, then ask a supplied policy to transform the subtotal. `NoDiscountStrategy` and `HolidayDiscountStrategy` implement the same `IDiscountStrategy` contract, so the caller can choose a discount without changing `TotalCalculator`. The variable algorithm is the discount; summing and returning the final total remain fixed. This is Strategy in its classic object-oriented form. The shorthand expresses the same design with a `Func<decimal, decimal>`. Its statement lambda receives a `decimal` and returns a `decimal`; the final expression lambda removes the braces and implicit `return`. Neither lambda captures outside state. In Python, a named function is already a first-class callable and is often the clearest strategy. Strategy names the design role, a higher-order function is the mechanism used by `Calculate`, and dependency injection describes supplying the policy from outside. These related labels are not synonyms.
concepts.caution: Do not create a class hierarchy for every one-line variation. Prefer named callables when they express the policy clearly, but use explicit strategy types when policies carry configuration, lifecycle, or several related operations.
concepts.related: State; Template Method; Dependency Injection; Higher-Order Function

concepts.title: Template Method
concepts.definition: Template Method defines a fixed algorithm sequence in a base class while allowing subclasses to replace selected steps.
concepts.look_for: Use it when policy requires one stable sequence and subclasses need only a few narrow, compile-time variation points.
concepts.walkthrough: `ImportJob.Run` is the template method. It permanently orders `Parse`, `Validate`, and `Save`, so every importer follows the same high-level process. `CsvImportJob` supplies the required parsing and persistence steps, while it inherits the default no-op `Validate` hook. The invariant sequence belongs to the base class; only the declared hooks vary. That is the pattern's central trade: subclasses cannot accidentally reorder the mandated workflow, but variation is tied to inheritance and type construction. Strategy solves a nearby problem through composition: callers can supply and rearrange independent policies at runtime. A pipeline of functions is often preferable when steps need dynamic composition, while Template Method remains useful when the sequence itself is an enforceable rule and subclasses form a stable family. The C# and Python examples deliberately use full method bodies so the fixed call order is visible.
concepts.caution: Too many hooks produce fragile base classes whose subclasses depend on undocumented call timing. Keep the template small, state hook preconditions, and prefer composition when variations must evolve independently.

concepts.title: Visitor
concepts.definition: Visitor places an operation outside a stable family of element types and uses double dispatch so each concrete element selects the matching operation.
concepts.look_for: Use it when element types change rarely but new operations across all those types arrive often, and those operations do not belong naturally inside the elements.
concepts.walkthrough: `Book.Accept` calls `visitor.Visit(this)`, and because `this` is statically a `Book` inside that class, overload resolution selects `TaxVisitor.Visit(Book)`. `Food.Accept` selects `Visit(Food)`. The first dispatch chooses the element's `Accept`; the second chooses the visitor overload, allowing `TaxVisitor` to keep type-specific tax logic outside the product classes. Adding another operation means adding another visitor without editing `Book` or `Food`. Adding a new product type, however, requires changing every visitor contract and implementation. That trade makes Visitor appropriate only when the element family is substantially more stable than the operations. C# pattern matching is often a simpler modern alternative for a closed union, while Python's `singledispatch` supplies runtime generic-function dispatch without explicit `accept` methods. Those alternatives provide similar type-based operation selection but are not the classic object-oriented double-dispatch structure.
concepts.caution: Visitor reverses the usual extension trade-off: new operations are easy, new element types are expensive. It can also break encapsulation if visitors need every internal detail of an element.
concepts.modern_note: Discriminated unions and exhaustive pattern matching often replace Visitor when the language can model a closed set of element cases directly.

concepts.title: Interpreter
concepts.definition: Interpreter represents a small language's grammar as expression objects whose recursive evaluation or translation gives meaning to a sentence in that language.
concepts.look_for: Use it for a tiny, stable rule or expression language; use a parser library or established language once precedence, diagnostics, tooling, or grammar growth becomes substantial.
concepts.walkthrough: `NumberExpression` represents the grammar's terminal number and evaluates directly to `_value`. `AddExpression` represents a production containing two child expressions; its `Evaluate` recursively interprets the left and right subtrees, then applies addition. The object graph for `2 + 3` is therefore also the program's abstract syntax tree. New expression classes extend the small language, while callers depend only on `IExpression`. This is the classic Interpreter pattern, not merely parsing: a parser would turn text into this tree, and these nodes supply the language's semantics. The same tree could instead be translated into SQL or another target. The approach is attractive for a handful of stable rules because grammar and behavior are visibly paired. It becomes unwieldy when a real language needs precedence, error recovery, source locations, optimization, or secure resource limits.
concepts.caution: Hand-rolled languages grow faster than expected. Never evaluate untrusted host-language code, bound recursion and resource use, and move to established parsing and evaluation tools before the grammar becomes infrastructure.
concepts.modern_note: This GoF pattern completes the classic catalog; parser combinators and generated parsers are usually better foundations for nontrivial languages.
